title: The Work of Christ
summary: What Jesus accomplished: His perfect life, atoning death, resurrection, ascension and ongoing intercession.
description: Why did Jesus die, and what did His death achieve? This course explains why atonement was necessary, the meaning of Christ's sacrifice as our substitute, the many biblical pictures of the cross (redemption, propitiation, reconciliation and victory), the importance of the resurrection and ascension, and the different views Christians hold on the extent of the atonement.
objectives: Explain why sin required an atonement
Teach the substitutionary nature of Christ's death
Explain the main biblical pictures of the atonement
Show the meaning of the resurrection and ascension
Present fairly the views on the extent of the atonement
outcomes: Explain how God can be both just and the justifier
Show how Old Testament sacrifices point to the cross
Give evidence for and the significance of the resurrection
Compare limited and unlimited atonement fairly

modules.title: Why the Cross Was Necessary
modules.intro: Could God simply forgive without the cross? This week we see why atonement was needed.

lessons.title: A holy God and sinful people
lessons.body:
God is holy and just; He "will by no means clear the guilty" (Exodus 34:7). Sin deserves death (Romans 6:23). A judge who ignores crime is not good.

Yet God is also love, and desires to save. How can He forgive sinners without denying His justice?

The answer is the cross. God set forth Christ "to be a propitiation... to declare his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus" (Romans 3:25-26). At the cross, sin is truly punished and sinners are truly forgiven.

lessons.title: Without shedding of blood
lessons.body:
Throughout the Old Testament, God taught that sin brings death and that a substitute could die in the sinner's place. "The life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul" (Leviticus 17:11).

"Without shedding of blood is no remission" (Hebrews 9:22). Yet "it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins" (Hebrews 10:4). The sacrifices were shadows pointing to a better sacrifice.

John the Baptist announced Him: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (John 1:29).

lessons.title: The obedient life
lessons.body:
Christ's saving work includes His perfect life as well as His death. He was "made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law" (Galatians 4:4-5). He said, "thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness" (Matthew 3:15).

Where Adam disobeyed, Christ obeyed: "by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous" (Romans 5:19). He became "obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (Philippians 2:8).

His spotless life qualified Him to be the Lamb "without blemish and without spot" (1 Peter 1:19), and His righteousness is credited to those who believe.

terms.def: The work by which Christ reconciled sinners to God through His death.
God's perfect rightness, which requires that sin be punished.
Forgiveness; the sending away of sin.
John's title for Jesus as the sacrifice who takes away sin.
Christ's perfect keeping of God's law throughout His life.
Christ's willing submission to suffering and death for our sins.

texts.teaches: God will by no means clear the guilty.
God is just and the justifier of him who believes in Jesus.
It is the blood that makes atonement for the soul.
The blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins.
By the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.

summary: God's justice requires that sin be punished; His love desires to save.
At the cross, God is both just and the justifier.
Old Testament sacrifices pointed to Christ, the Lamb of God.
Christ's perfect obedient life is part of His saving work.

options: The blood of bulls and goats

modules.title: He Died for Us
modules.intro: This week we study the heart of the atonement: Christ died as our substitute, bearing the penalty of our sin.

lessons.title: Isaiah 53: the suffering Servant
lessons.body:
Seven centuries before the cross, Isaiah described a Servant who would suffer for others:

"He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray... and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:5-6).

Notice the words *for us* and *laid on him*. The Servant bears the sins of others and makes "his soul an offering for sin" (53:10). Philip used this passage to preach Jesus to the Ethiopian (Acts 8:32-35).

lessons.title: Substitution
lessons.body:
The New Testament repeatedly says Christ died **for** us, in our place:

- "Christ died for our sins" (1 Corinthians 15:3).
- "He hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him" (2 Corinthians 5:21).
- "Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God" (1 Peter 3:18).
- "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13).

This is called **penal substitution**: Christ bore the penalty our sins deserved.

lessons.title: My God, why hast thou forsaken me?
lessons.body:
On the cross Jesus cried, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). He experienced the separation from God that sin deserves, as He bore our sins in His own body (1 Peter 2:24).

Then He cried, "It is finished" (John 19:30). The Greek word was used for a debt paid in full. Nothing remains to be added to His work.

The cross shows both how serious sin is and how great God's love is: "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (1 John 4:10).

terms.def: Christ taking our place and dying for us.
Christ bearing the penalty that our sins deserved.
Isaiah's figure who bears the sins of many, fulfilled in Christ.
Crediting one person's record to another: our sin to Christ, His righteousness to us.
Christ's cry from the cross declaring His work complete, a debt paid in full.
The condemnation the law pronounces on lawbreakers, which Christ bore.

Christ died as our substitute, bearing the penalty of our sin.
On the cross He was forsaken so that we might be accepted.

options: His saving work was complete, the debt paid

options: They are made the righteousness of God in Christ

modules.title: Pictures of the Cross
modules.intro: The Bible uses several pictures to describe what Christ's death achieved. This week we study four of them.

lessons.title: Propitiation and redemption
lessons.body:
**Propitiation** means turning away wrath by a sacrifice. God's righteous anger against sin is real (Romans 1:18). Christ is "the propitiation for our sins" (1 John 2:2); God's wrath fell on Him, so it does not fall on believers.

**Redemption** comes from the marketplace: buying back a slave by paying a price. "Ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold... But with the precious blood of Christ" (1 Peter 1:18-19). The Son of man came "to give his life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45).

Believers are no longer their own; they were "bought with a price" (1 Corinthians 6:20).

lessons.title: Reconciliation
lessons.body:
**Reconciliation** is from the language of relationships: enemies made friends. Sin made us "enemies" of God (Romans 5:10) and "alienated" from Him (Colossians 1:21).

Through Christ, "God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them" (2 Corinthians 5:19). Peace with God is now offered: "Being justified by faith, we have peace with God" (Romans 5:1).

The cross also reconciles people to one another, breaking down walls between Jew and Gentile and making "one new man" (Ephesians 2:14-16). This is the ministry of reconciliation given to us (2 Corinthians 5:18).

lessons.title: Victory and example
lessons.body:
**Victory:** the cross defeated Satan, sin and death. Christ "spoiled principalities and powers... triumphing over them in it" (Colossians 2:15); through death He destroyed "him that had the power of death" (Hebrews 2:14).

**Example:** Christ suffered "leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps" (1 Peter 2:21), showing perfect love, forgiveness and obedience.

These pictures complete one another. But the example and victory rest on substitution: Christ defeats Satan by removing our guilt, and we can follow Him only because He first died for us.

terms.def: A sacrifice that turns away God's wrath against sin.
Being bought back from slavery by the payment of a price.
The price paid to set captives free; Christ's life.
Restoring peace between enemies; between God and sinners.
The picture of the cross as Christ's victory over Satan, sin and death.
Christ's death as a pattern of love and obedience for us to follow.

texts.teaches: Christ is the propitiation for our sins.
Believers are redeemed with the precious blood of Christ.
The Son of man gave His life a ransom for many.
God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself.
Christ suffered, leaving us an example to follow.

summary: Propitiation: Christ turned away God's wrath.
Redemption: Christ bought us back with His blood.
Reconciliation: Christ made enemies into friends of God and of one another.
Victory and example rest on His substitutionary death.

questions.q: What does propitiation mean?
options: A sacrifice that turns away wrath

options: We can follow Christ only because He first died for us

modules.title: Risen and Ascended
modules.intro: The cross is not the end. This week we study Christ's resurrection, ascension and present ministry.

lessons.title: He is risen indeed
lessons.body:
Christ rose bodily on the third day. The tomb was empty; He appeared many times to many witnesses, including over five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:3-8). The disciples, once fearful, boldly preached and died for this truth.

The resurrection is essential: "if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins" (1 Corinthians 15:17).

It proves Jesus is the Son of God (Romans 1:4), shows the Father accepted His sacrifice (Romans 4:25), guarantees our justification and our future resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20-23), and defeats death.

lessons.title: Ascended to the right hand
lessons.body:
Forty days after rising, Jesus ascended to heaven from the Mount of Olives (Acts 1:9-11). He "sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high" (Hebrews 1:3), the place of honour and authority.

His sitting shows His sacrifice is complete: unlike priests who stood daily, "this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down" (Hebrews 10:12).

From there He poured out the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:33), rules over all things for the church (Ephesians 1:22) and will return in the same way He went (Acts 1:11).

lessons.title: He ever lives to intercede
lessons.body:
Christ's work continues in heaven. He "ever liveth to make intercession" for those who come to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25). "If any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous" (1 John 2:1).

"Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us" (Romans 8:34).

So believers can "come boldly unto the throne of grace" (Hebrews 4:16), confident that our living Saviour represents us.

Christ's resurrection as the first part and guarantee of the harvest of believers' resurrection.

The place of supreme honour and authority.

modules.title: For Whom Did Christ Die?
modules.intro: Christians agree that Christ's death is sufficient for all and effective for believers. They differ on its design. This week we study the views fairly and apply the cross.

lessons.title: Unlimited (general) atonement
lessons.body:
Many Christians, including many Baptists, Wesleyans and Holiness and Pentecostal churches such as Deeper Life, hold that Christ died for every person, making salvation possible for all, though only those who believe receive it.

They point to texts such as: "he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2:2); Christ "gave himself a ransom for all" (1 Timothy 2:6); He "tasted death for every man" (Hebrews 2:9); and God is "not willing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9).

On this view the gospel offer is sincere to all because Christ truly died for all.

lessons.title: Limited (particular) atonement
lessons.body:
Reformed Christians, including Reformed Baptists, hold that Christ died with the specific purpose of saving the elect, and that His death actually secures their salvation. This is also called **definite** or **particular** atonement.

They point to texts such as: "I lay down my life for the sheep" (John 10:15); Christ "loved the church, and gave himself for it" (Ephesians 5:25); "he shall save his people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21); He bore "the sins of many" (Hebrews 9:28).

They too affirm that Christ's death is sufficient for all and that the gospel must be freely offered to everyone.

lessons.title: Common ground and response
lessons.body:
Both views agree on vital points: Christ's death is of infinite worth, sufficient for all; only those who repent and believe are saved; the gospel must be preached to every creature (Mark 16:15); and no one who comes to Christ will be turned away (John 6:37).

The proper response to the cross is not debate but faith, gratitude and a changed life. "The love of Christ constraineth us... that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again" (2 Corinthians 5:14-15).

Isaac Watts' hymn says it well: "Love so amazing, so divine, demands my soul, my life, my all."

terms.def: The question of for whom Christ died, and with what purpose.
The view that Christ died for every person, making salvation possible for all.
The view that Christ died specifically to secure the salvation of the elect.
Christ's death has infinite worth, enough to save everyone.
Christ's death actually saves those who believe.
The sincere invitation to all people to repent and believe.

texts.teaches: Christ is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world.
Christ gave Himself a ransom for all.
The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
Whoever comes to Christ will in no wise be cast out.
Those who live should live for Him who died for them.

summary: Unlimited atonement: Christ died for all, making salvation possible for all.
Limited atonement: Christ died to secure the salvation of the elect.
Both agree His death is sufficient for all and the gospel must be offered to all.
The right response to the cross is faith, gratitude and a life for Christ.

options: The gospel must be offered to all and Christ's death is sufficient for all

short.q: Why was the cross necessary for God to forgive sinners?
short.model: God is just and must punish sin, yet in love desires to forgive; at the cross Christ bore the punishment so God is both just and the justifier.

short.q: Explain penal substitution with one Bible reference.
short.model: Christ took our place and bore the penalty our sins deserved, as in 1 Peter 3:18: the just for the unjust.
Propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God's wrath; redemption is buying back a slave by paying a price, Christ's blood.

short.q: Give three reasons the resurrection matters.
short.model: It proves Jesus is the Son of God, shows God accepted His sacrifice for our justification, and guarantees our own resurrection.

short.q: What does Christ do for believers now in heaven?
short.model: He intercedes for us as our advocate at the Father's right hand, and rules over all things for the church.

short.q: Compare limited and unlimited atonement fairly.
short.model: Unlimited atonement says Christ died for all, making salvation possible; limited atonement says He died to secure the elect's salvation. Both agree His death is sufficient for all and the gospel is offered to all.

assignments.title: The cross in the Old Testament
assignments.prompt: Choose two Old Testament passages or practices that point to the cross (for example the Passover, the Day of Atonement, the bronze serpent or Isaiah 53). Explain each and show how the New Testament applies it to Christ's work.

assignments.title: Why did Jesus die?
assignments.prompt: Write a clear answer to a young person who asks, "Why did Jesus have to die? Couldn't God just forgive?" Use at least five passages from the course and the pictures of propitiation, redemption and reconciliation.
